utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Can we have the appearances, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honours please, my name is Niemann and I appear with my colleagues Ms. McHenry, Mr. Turone and Mr. Khan for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: And the appearances for the Defence, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I am Edina Residovic, Defence counsel for Mr. Zejnil Delalic, together with my colleague, Eugene O'Sullivan, professor from Canada. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I am Zeljko Olujic, Defence counsel from Croatia, Defence counsel of Mr. Zdravko Mucic, together with my colleague, Michael Greaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I am Salih Karabdic, attorney from Sarajevo, Defence counsel of Mr. Hazim Delic, together with my colleague Thomas Moran, attorney from Houston, Texas.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours, I am John Ackerman, I am here on behalf of Esad Landzo, along with my co-counsel Cynthia McMurrey.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I would like to take the Prosecution's motion for an order requiring advance disclosure of witnesses by the Defence. Can we hear the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honours please, the Prosecution relies on the submissions it sets out in writing in its motion. We have not received any response from the Defence and that may be so because we, the Prosecution, throughout the course of the Prosecution case has been punctilious in providing notice, not only at the outset of the witnesses that we intended to call, but also during the course of the trial, provided notice at 14 day intervals and then on seven day intervals in relation to the order of which witnesses were called. Circumstances beyond our control occasionally required us to change order of witnesses, but in the vast majority of instances, the notices were complied with and were provided in time. Your Honours, the notices were required because the Defence had brought to your attention on numerous occasions the fact that they would have been inhibited in their cross-examination of witnesses if they did not have notice of who it was that we were going to call and intimated that, of course, if they did not know who was next to be called by the Prosecution that they could not proceed to deal with the cross-examination there and then because they needed the time in order to prepare. So, your Honours, we can only assume from the fact that there has been no response from them that they agree with our motion and that it represents common sense and it is reasonable in terms of organising the orderly conduct of the trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Do we have any reaction from the Defence, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: May it please your Honour, this is an issue which your Honours have already decided. Can I remind you of what you were doing on 21st February 1997? You were deciding on that occasion this very issue. On 21st February 1997, the question of whether the Defence should be obliged to disclose either the names and addresses of witnesses, or the statements of witnesses, was conclusively decided. I say conclusively because I would remind your Honours of a ruling that you gave on 25th September of last year. During the course of that decision, you concluded that you were functus officio once a matter had been decided, that you were not an appellate or review entity. What you said in your order of 25th September 1997, paragraph 43, is this: "The Trial Chamber is not an appellate or review entity. The Trial Chamber is functus officio once a matter has been decided, and no measure of repetition or recloaking of an argument can authorise it to act in excess of its jurisdiction. The Trial Chamber declines to exercise a jurisdiction it does not possess." We respectfully submit that your Honours have already determined this issue and that you have no power to entertain a further motion from the Prosecution at this stage, effectively, to overturn your own order. If I am wrong about that, I would respectfully remind your Honours of this: the Rules of Procedure and Evidence were framed, and my understanding is that it was your Honours, being the first judges of this Tribunal, who had the task of drawing up together a set of rules to govern the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. During the course of that period, that exercise, your Honours had an opportunity to deal with this very question. How did your Honours deal with it? Can I remind your Honours of Rule 67? Rule 67 comes in a section which is headed "pre-trial proceedings". It is called, "Rule 67: reciprocal disclosure". Your Honours concluded that the appropriate way to deal with reciprocal disclosure was through the Rule that has been set out. The relevant parts of the Rule, for the purposes of this argument, are Rule 67(A), and that is (A)(i) and (A)(ii), and Rule 67(C). We respectfully submit that the process of rule making led to the conclusion that the only elements of reciprocal disclosure should be those that are set out in the Rule. If your Honours had decided that there was to be a rule requiring the Defence to disclose either the names and addresses of its witnesses, or its witness statements, to the Prosecution, there was both the opportunity to include such an order and it should have been set out clearly. Plainly, no such decision was taken. There is nowhere in the Rules any requirement authorising your Honours to say to the Defence, "you must disclose your names and addresses of witnesses and witness statements to the Prosecution". That is the very order to which your Honours -- conclusion to which your Honours came in February of last year. The only requirement that the rule makers decided should be imposed upon the Defence is that set out in Rule 67(A)(ii), "alibi or special defence". No other requirement was decided by the rule makers as being appropriate. There is no such rule. Can I remind your Honours of what you said in your order of 21st February of last year? Paragraph 9: "Rule 66 and Rule 67 set forth specific obligations relating to the disclosure of evidence. The general provisions of Rule 54 may not be used to circumvent specific requirements enunciated in those Rules." Paragraph 10: "The Trial Chamber accepts the submission of the Defence that under the Rules there is no general reciprocal obligation on the Defence to give notice to the Prosecution of witnesses it intends to call at trial. Sub-rule 67(A)(ii), however, imposes such an obligation on the Defence when it intends to offer a defence of alibi or any other special defence, including that of diminished or lack of mental responsibility." 11: "The Defence of the accused Zejnil Delalic has not given notice of it to offer any of the defences contemplated by sub-rule 67(A)(ii). The Trial Chamber therefore accepts its submission that at the present time it is not obliged to provide a witness list for the Prosecution." We respectfully submit that your Honours took a clear and proper decision on the Rules, because it is the Rules of Procedure and Evidence which determine your Honours' powers. You have quite clearly stated in that decision firstly the only obligation is to disclose alibi witnesses, special defence witnesses. Rule 54 may not be used to get round Rule 67. In their application, in their motion, that is what the Prosecution are now inviting you to do. We respectfully submit that you already ruled and said, "you cannot do that". Effectively what they are trying to do is to use your Honours as an appeal or review entity. We respectfully submit that is outside your Honours' powers. They refer to the Dokmanovic case. I say this about the decision in that case. Firstly, there was no power in that Trial Chamber, just as there is no power in this Trial Chamber, to make such an order. If the Defence in that case agreed to such an order, I can well imagine that if I had the task of advising Mr. Dokmanovic on an appeal, I would be telling him that for the Defence to have agreed to what was agreed to in that case was negligent and he should not have done it, because what he was doing was assisting the Prosecution, and in pretty well every jurisdiction, for the Defence to assist the Prosecution in that way must be negligent. Rule 67 and Rule 54 are quite clear, we submit. Rule 67 is a rule of specific application. It plainly is intended to apply to the question of reciprocal disclosure and to set out the Trial Chamber's powers in relation to reciprocal disclosure and to be exhaustive of your Honours' powers. Rule 54 cannot be used in that way. The Prosecution say this in their motion, that if you do not do that, if you do not do as they wish, they will be forced to apply for an adjournment after every witness. They plainly have the right to do that. Of course, they can do it. They will have, if they wish to do that, to justify it to your Honours on a case-by-case basis. Your Honours will recall before Christmas, in the case of Professor Economides that the Defence as a whole applied to your Honours for an adjournment, justified that adjournment and your Honours granted it. Plainly it is right that they have that opportunity, but they should know that they will have to justify each application for an adjournment. We respectfully submit that in the absence of any express power to order this, this motion should be rejected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Can we hear your reaction?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Your Honour, firstly accusing counsel briefed in another case of negligence, your Honours, is a most inappropriate and unsatisfactory thing to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You can ignore that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Let us see what the legal rights of the accused are. Are they bound to provide you with a list of witnesses before they enter upon their defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If I may deal with the issues, your Honour? Firstly it was raised that your Honours had already made an order and true that is, that in a pre-trial context your Honours did make an order. To suggest then that interlocutory orders are final and can never be varied is something peculiar, at least to my understanding of interlocutory orders. Interlocutory orders deal with the situation at the moment, within the confines of the case, and there are numerous instances where interlocutory orders have subsequently been changed, especially during the course of the proceeding -- during the course of the proceedings of one of the parties, so as the Prosecution has not closed its case, it is our submission that changed circumstances is and has always been recognised as a justifiable basis for revisiting interlocutory orders. There are changed circumstances, your Honours, in our respectful submission. A Trial Chamber has on two occasions ordered pre-trial discovery, and so that is something different to what was the position at the time when we filed our original motion, so to answer your Honours' question, we say yes, there is now a power within your Honours to make such an order. Your Honours have the power to do it under Rule 54. To argue that Rule 67 somehow or other deals with the matter to the exclusion of all other of your Honours' powers in our submission is quite incorrect. Rule 67 deals with a specific circumstance. It expresses itself on that circumstance. An order under Rule 54 would not in our submission in any way seek to override the operation or interfere with the operation of Rule 67. It would not do that at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Surely they would provide you with the list when they enter upon their defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, that is not something that I hear coming from the Defence. If they are to say that that is what they are prepared to do, seven days before they call the witnesses, and that is something they are happily agreed to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: But Mr. Greaves, you will provide a list of witnesses when you enter upon a defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: No. There is no requirement in the Rules for us to do that, we say, absolutely none. There is no power whatever, we say, to order us to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: So you will produce witnesses by way of surprise.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I am not sure this is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: We say that there is no power whatever for your Honours to order us to provide at any stage a list of witnesses. If the Rules had been intended to do that, it would be expressly stated in it. There were two circumstances which the rule makers decided were appropriate for the disclosure of witnesses, those are 67(A)(ii), alibi and special defence. In no other circumstance do the Rules contemplate us being ordered to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Is there a provision that gives you the right to withhold the names of your witnesses until they actually appear in the court?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: No, the Rules are silent about that. It may well be that is because the matter was considered to be exhaustively dealt with by Rule 67.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Mr. Greaves, let us try and construe Rule 67(A)(i) and (ii). If you read (A) carefully, it says: "As early as reasonably practicable and in any event prior to the commencement of the trial." Those are the limiting words, "prior to the commencement of the trial". Then it goes on to tell you what the Prosecution should do. Now (A)(ii) talks about the defences which mandatorily must be notified. It did not say that there can be no notification in respect of other matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: No, the point I make is this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: It did not say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: The issue of what should be within your Honours' powers to order was considered. If it had been the intention of the rule makers to permit an order for the disclosure of witness lists by the Defence, it would have been expressly stated. In the absence of an express statement that you have that power, we say you do not have the power.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I am trying to point out to you the ordinary construction any lawyer would give to Rule 67(A)(i) and (ii). Where (A)(ii) refers to specific cases where notification is mandatory, it did not rule out notification in other cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: No, it does not say one way or the other, but if it had been the intention of the rule makers to make such an order --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: That is the issue. If it is an open-ended question and if you look at our decision on 21st February at paragraph 11, the words used: "We accept the submission of the Defence at the present time it is not obliged to provide a witness list to the Prosecution." "At the present time". It does not mean that when trial has commenced, as in this case, it could not. Every word used in a legislation is material. You have to construe them in accordance with the words so used. I agree there are favourable interpretations if you perhaps leave out certain phrases, but when construed as a whole, you will find that some of these things have been taken into account.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I beg to differ, if your Honour is saying that there is any express power.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Not express power, but it is implied from the provisions themselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Apart from that, if the Rules are silent, we have to adopt a procedure which leads to a fair trial; just like the Defence should not be taken by surprise, the Prosecution should also not be taken by surprise. We only ask you to produce your list of witnesses when you enter upon your defence, not before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: One would like to examine that. Is it fair to order the Defence effectively to disclose its defence?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Not earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Bearing in mind the burden of proof, one has to remember there is no obligation on the Defence in a fair trial where the burden of proof is placed upon the Prosecution and the standard of proof is that of beyond reasonable doubt, there is no obligation on the Defence to be put in the position of assisting the Prosecution. Your Honours have already dealt with that in the question of handwriting and Mr. Mucic, and effectively making such an order would be ordering us to assist the Prosecution. That is not, we respectfully submit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think you are pushing this question of equality too far, at least you are making it difficult for the Prosecution also to challenge your own witnesses, if they have doubts. If they really have any doubts, they should know who these witnesses are and they should be able to say something about them. If they know nothing about them, it is difficult for them to effectively challenge them. I think you agree with that, if that is a Prosecution witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Plainly from the point of view of the Prosecution, it does not assist them at all. For a defendant, this is not about assisting the Prosecution to help him be convicted. That is the point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: No, it does not. At least his credibility could be in doubt and that is part of the Prosecution's case, to state quite clearly who is the person coming to say something.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I suspect we may not be ad idem on this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: The entire Defence case is part of the Prosecution's case.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I am sorry, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Perhaps you might not understand that, but the Prosecution has to prove his case beyond reasonable doubt, including the case of the Defence, and he should know exactly what the Defence is coming to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I join in this discussion, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You may.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I completely second the arguments submitted by my colleague, Michael Greaves, and would like to add a couple of things before this Trial Chamber, in order to support the arguments put forward by my colleague, Greaves. My arguments are going to rest on the Article 20 of the Statute. Let me remind you of this provision from the Statute. We shall see that a fair trial can only be ensured if it is done according to the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. We have to follow the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, and in this way, we will ensure a fair trial. The moment we try to define the position of one of the sides based on another, then we are on a very dangerous ground. Why am I saying this? It is true that the Trial Chamber on several occasions has obligated the Prosecutor to produce the witness list to the Defence in due time, but the Trial Chamber did not do this in order to make the position of the Defence easier, but because it is the right of the Defence set out by the Statute and the Rules. Your Honours, I am going to remind you again of Article 21, where the minimum rights of the accused have been set, which have to be respected in these proceedings. First, it is that the accused is presumed innocent. This basic right makes it incumbent upon the Prosecution to prove his guilt and does not imply that the Defence is obligated in any way to assist the Prosecution in doing this. Then we have Article 21(4)(b), in which it is stated that the accused will have adequate time and facilities for the preparation of his defence and to communicate with the counsel of his own choosing. This right of the accused in the criminal proceedings obliges the Prosecutor to allow the accused sufficient time and enables the Trial Chamber, should the Prosecution fail to do so, to allow for enough time for the accused to prepare his defence, and to cross-examine. Similar provisions, with respect to Defence, is not reciprocal when it refers to the Prosecution and its preparation for the cross-examination of the Defence witnesses. We have the issue of the fair trial here. The Rule that I just mentioned is virtually the only right of the accused to have some kind of parity and to prepare to respond to the powers that the Prosecution has over the accused. If you look at the Statute and the Rules, you will see that the Prosecution is assisted by many bodies, the United Nations, international organisations, Interpol, individual states, and the accused has no such institution to assist him in preparation of his own defence. This is why the Prosecution does not have the right to request of the Defence assistance in order to support his case. I would like to remind you, your Honours, that since this Tribunal was established until March 1995, the Prosecution had enough time, ample time until March 18th, the date when my client was arrested, they had enough time to prepare for presenting its case and to prepare for responding to the preparation of the defence. So reading expressly all the provisions of the Statute and the Rules, it is clear that the Defence has no obligation to provide a witness list to the Prosecution and the Prosecution should feel at no time that any witness that is brought forth by the Defence is a surprise. I would also like to say that you judged wisely when you ruled that the Defence had no obligation to provide witness lists to the Prosecution, and I think that following the rights of the accused, you will confirm this decision, and will not obligate the Defence beyond what the provisions of the Statute and the Rules already imply that the Defence should do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, might I respond?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Would you not prefer the Defence concluding before you respond?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It would be easier for me to respond to each one as they come up. If your Honours prefer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: If it is more convenient for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think it would be better, your Honours. Your Honours the issue about it not being a fair trial, that has nothing to do with whether or not it is a fair trial, this is a case of the orderly conduct of the proceedings. It has nothing to do with assisting the Prosecution in meeting its burden. That should be done in the Prosecution's case. It has nothing to do with that at all. So, your Honours, then to suggest that the Prosecution has all these vast resources at its disposal which therefore somehow or other justifies an approach which would not permit an orderly conduct of the trial does not, in my submission, add up. Firstly, the Prosecution does not have all these resources at its disposal at all and I think it is notorious how difficult matters are for the Prosecution because of the way things are structured. Secondly, it is in everybody's interest that the trial proceed in an orderly fashion. There can only be one justification or one reason why the Defence are mounting this argument, and that is because they want the element of surprise, of ambush, to be able to spring things on in a situation where the Prosecution is not going to be able to respond immediately. Therefore we are going to be pushed into a situation of continuously seeking adjournments to allow us to investigate matters. All of this can be circumvented, in our submission, if a very sensible order is made under Rule 54 for them to provide notice of the witnesses they intend to call. I emphasise, and I pick up upon what your Honour Judge Karibi-Whyte has said, it has nothing to do whatsoever with Rule 67. Rule 67 has finished, it has no more application in these proceedings. So there is only one Rule left and that is Rule 54. It is not Rule 67 being overridden by Rule 54 at all. It is your Honours making a decision for the orderly conduct of the trial which is expressly permitted under Rule 54, because it says that is what you can do. So in our submission, your Honours, to suggest that somehow or other to make an order this would interfere with the right of a fair trial and would assist the Prosecution in meeting its burden is an absurd argument.

utterances.speaker: MISS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honours -- which one?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Mr. Moran. After Moran then you can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You are number four, he is number two in the list of accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, just a couple of quick thoughts on this. First, I have been informed by my colleagues from the former Yugoslavia that prior to my involvement in this case, that is more than a year ago, substantial material was turned over by the Defence voluntarily to the Office of the Prosecutor in the form of witness statements, things like that. I have not seen a list of what was turned over, but I am told that it is fairly substantial, is that correct? With that, I do not think that there should be much surprise, since they have had statements in their hands for a year. My other thought on it is this, and I will defer to Mr. Niemann on the actual specifics of it, but, as I understand it, Trial Chamber I, that is this Trial Chamber, in the Tadic case, held that Rules 60 through 70 set two different requirements for disclosure and that there is no requirement for the Defence to turn over things like witness statements or witness lists. We have been trying, one of my colleagues has been trying to get a copy of the Prosecutor's Notice of Appeal, we understand that is a confidential document in the Tadic case, but if the Prosecutor was not happy with that ruling from Trial Chamber I, they should have appealed it. Although there are different judges, it is the same Trial Chamber and I would suggest that you are bound by the prior ruling of Trial Chamber I. Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honours, we would like to also further support the arguments of our other colleagues at this point and also say that this is further complicated by the fact, of course, this defendant Mr. Landzo is the only one who has applied for a defence and therefore we want to assure the court that we intend to comply with Rule 67(ii)(b) in that matter. It is my understanding also that before I ever came into the case last year that the other attorney had turned over prior witness statements and witness lists to the Prosecutor way over a year ago, so there could not be a whole lot of surprise left for them at this point. Another complicating factor is I just returned from Bosnia in November and I spent time there interviewing witnesses, and based upon the prior holding of this court, of course I have a lot of witnesses that are very timid about appearing here in The Hague, and rightly so, and I have assured them that we will be seeking certain protections for them as we are allowed to do, but at the time that I interviewed them, I also assured them that I did not have to turn over their names to the Prosecution at this time, based upon your prior ruling. So it would mean that I would have to go back now to Bosnia and re-interview and renegotiate with these witnesses at this point before we could go further in preparation for our defence, and these witnesses are relying on my guarantee to them that our witness list would not be turned over at this point, so I would like the court to consider that as just another complicating factor in changing the rulings as we go through, although I do know that you have the ability to do so. The arguments put out by Mucic and Delalic and Delic at this point we support 100 per cent, and hope you will consider the predicament we are in at this point if we are forced to change our procedure at this point in the trial. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: (Inaudible).

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes, I will be asking for protective measures, but if the Prosecution wish to have the names right now, I would have to get it all done appropriately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It is only when you enter upon your defence because you have the right to produce your witnesses under the same conditions as the Prosecution has. If the Prosecution is entitled to protection for witnesses, you are entitled to the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, we are quite thankful for that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, before colleague Niemann responds, may I add another argument related to colleague Niemann's response to my previous arguments? May I proceed your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Let her conclude, so that you can reply all of them together. Yes, let us hear you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. Colleague Niemann referred in his response to the fact that the provisions of Rule 67 were applied to the pre-trial proceedings and that this Trial Chamber still has the ability to make rulings in accordance with Rule 54. In view of the fact that we have to strictly abide by the provisions of the Statute and the Rules, it follows that the provisions of Rule 67 is lex specialis in relation to Rule 54 and I wish to underline that both Rules 54 and 67 are in the same section of the Rules, which means in the fifth chapter entitled, "prior procedure" -- "preliminary procedures". Therefore this Rule could be said to apply to a previous stage of the proceedings. If the Prosecutor feels that Rule 54 should be expanded to the actual trial, I think it is impossible to do that now, unless the limitations were to be spread out to the trial stage, that is the special provisions linked to Rule 54, like a lex specialis, according to the rule deroga legis specialis, then the provisions of Rule 67 should be treated in the same way as Rule 54. Also, Rule 85 allows the Trial Chamber to intervene in the presentation of evidence, but I also wish to draw attention to Rule 98, that the Trial Chamber may order production of additional evidence, but again it does not say anything as to the right of the Trial Chamber to oblige the Defence to submit witness lists outside the provisions of Rule 67.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Could I trade on my learned friend's patience? I know he is a patient man, for a moment, just to add one thing?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you may, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you very much, your Honour. It arises out of something that the learned judge, Judge Jan said about surprise. In the common law system, and I do not speak about the civil law system, I believe that the original exception to the disclosure of a defence came about in England in 1967, as a result of two sets of trials that were conducted against a set of gangsters, the Richardson gang and the Kray gang, who were notorious for producing bent witnesses, paid witnesses, who were sprung upon the Prosecution at the last minute. As a result of those trials, there was much comment in the press and in Parliament about so-called "ambush alibi defences". As a result of that, an exception to the general rule in English law, "are not bound to disclose your defence", was introduced and any practitioner in English law would recognise Rule 67(A)(ii) as being that kind of rule. I suspect that elsewhere in the common law system, other jurisdictions followed that in due course. The point I make is this, that an alibi defence is an ambush defence, and the Rules have contemplated one specific ambush or surprise defence as being worthy of pre -- reciprocal disclosure. So plainly the Rules contemplate this alibi defence as the one piece of surprise that has to be disclosed. If the Rules had intended to make all surprises to be removed, it would have said so. Of course, this is a defence which is given during the course of the Defence case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I mis-spoke as to something and I do not know if I owe an apology to this Trial Chamber or Trial Chamber I, I know darn well this is Trial Chamber II, I blame it on jet lag, but it is the same as the Tadic Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: As Mr. Moran has risen to deal with that issue, I will deal with it first. I suggest your Honours follow what happened in the Tadic case. What happened in the Tadic case was the Prosecution sought an order from the court that we be given witness statements. It was that that the court ruled we were not permitted to have, after originally ordering that we could have them, but the list of witnesses was always provided to the Prosecution during the course of that case, so that matter that has been urged upon your Honour I support and reinforce and suggest that your Honours follow what happened in Tadic, and that is that the Defence provide the list of witnesses. Your Honours, dealing with the matter raised by Mr. Greaves in dealing with Rule 67, Rule 67, your Honours, is a Rule which permits investigation of an alibi defence, hence its requirement prior to the commencement of trial, because there is difficulty in conducting investigation into the defence of alibi unless a large amount of notice is given to permit that to happen. That is why it appears in the way it does. It is interesting to note that if there is some notion that providing the Prosecution with notice of a defence represents an infringement on the right of a fair trial, then presumably this notice would do that, and yet I suggest, your Honours, that there is no such thing as infringing the right of a fair trial, and that is why it is permissible to have a rule such as Rule 67(A), because it does not in any way infringe. Your Honours, the issue of whether Rule 54 -- it has been suggested by Madam Residovic that that Rule only applies pre-trial. It clearly does not. The reading of the Rule is very clear. It says in the very last four words of the Rule, "conduct of the trial" and conduct of the trial is something that can happen at any stage during the course of the trial. Your Honours, it has been suggested that in some way the United Kingdom leads the field in terms of providing for alibi notices under Rule 67(A) of our Rules. I am sorry to disappoint my friend, but rules such as Rule 67 have been about for some time and I believe that practitioners in the United States would be well familiar in the federal jurisdiction of having to provide witness lists. I understand from my colleagues that come from that jurisdiction that that is a regular thing and certainly in the jurisdiction that I come from, so if there is a suggestion that all common law jurisdictions somehow or other provide that such witness lists are not provided, then I suggest that the Defence conduct further investigation into this, because certainly in the jurisdiction I come from, it orders for the disclosure of the list of witnesses the Defence intend to call is regularly made by judges in cases and no one ever suggests that that somehow or other infringes upon the right of a fair trial. So if there is some prohibition about providing such lists, on the contrary to what has been suggested by Mr. Greaves, I would suggest that England is the exception and not the rule. There was reference made to Rule 85; frankly your Honours, I cannot assist you with anything on that matter, because I simply see -- I cannot see any basis upon which Rule 85 can be called in aid of a Defence argument in this matter. In our submission, your Honours, it all does go to whether or not there is to be an orderly presentation of the Defence case and Rule 54 permits you to do that. The Defence have made a lot during this case of the requirement of being given notice. They have done so because they have said they need it for preparation. They have pointed to absolutely nothing to suggest that the Prosecution is in any different position. We have heard suggestions made that witnesses have been approached, and that they are under a misapprehension that their names will not be revealed. Your Honours, there are ways of dealing with that, we understand that situation, and there is no reason why the Defence cannot prepare appropriate orders for this Chamber dealing with those witnesses, and they can be dealt with as an exception, and we can get on and litigate that question as soon as possible, and once resolved, we can then deal with the notice in respect of those witnesses. If a witness has been informed that their names will not be revealed, then in our submission that assumes that your Honours are not going to proceed to make orders for the orderly conduct of the trial, and so it may be regrettable for the witness, but that witness presumably has been given advice made on an assumption that your Honours are going to make an order in a particular way. In our submission, your Honours, this all goes to the orderly conduct of the case and we submit your Honours have ample power under Rule 54. We urge you to apply the Tadic case and order the Defence to supply a list of witnesses in a timely fashion prior to the calling of those witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think we will grant the application and I think we will give our reasons within the next few days. The Defence should file with the Prosecution a list of its witnesses it intends to use at the trial, at least seven days before the beginning of the hearing of the Defence case. I think the Defence is at -- it has the opportunity of applying for any protection which it wants its witnesses to have, with the usual guarantees if there is any reason why the protection is required, because the protection is in respect of witnesses and not limited to Prosecution witnesses. The Defence is entitled to the protection.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I just wanted to ask for clarification, your Honour. When you say seven days prior to the defence, that is each individual defence case, is that correct? Not when the defence starts its case in chief, but when Landzo starts his defence case? I just wanted to ask for clarification on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: For clarification, at least seven days before the witness itself comes on for his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: That was probably then what you were asking.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I will be happy with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am not arguing with the court's order, but I want the court to recall that at one point, we asked for the current addresses of Prosecution witnesses so that we could investigate whether they had been convicted of felonies and look into their reputations for truthfulness in the places where they currently reside. The Prosecution opposed that and the Trial Chamber went with the Prosecution on that. I would ask that the same --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Identifying material need not contain the present address.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You want to retaliate in giving ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is the sauce for the goose, sauce for the gander, rule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: If that suits you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I raise another question outside this subject matter, irrespective of this subject, because I take it that you have ruled on this matter now. During the closed session, I asked you to be kind enough to tell us, if possible, the date when we will receive your rulings in connection with the documents from Vienna, and the statements of the co-accused. We had expected to receive that by today, but I would appeal to you, if you could tell us with some precision, because Delalic's Defence cannot begin to prepare its submissions without that and we have already committed ourselves to preparing that within a certain time period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I am hoping you might get the rulings within the week, in the course of the week. Does that satisfy you, in the course of this week I am hoping you would get the rulings.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am satisfied, if it will be in the course of this week, without the addition that it will probably be in the course of this week, so that we might begin working on our own motions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I have never been as precise as "this week", I have always told you it was coming, but now I say in the course of this week.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I hope that you understand, because we were precise in saying that we will make our submissions three days after the cross-examination of Dr. Gow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The Trial Chamber will now rise. (12.10 pm)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
